curatorBrief.title: The Equal Sign and the Balance Scale
curatorBrief.intent: Welcome first-grade mathematicians to explore balance scales! Hook learners with the idea of a teeter-totter, introducing how balance means both sides have the exact same amount and previewing how we connect physical weights to the equal sign.

componentConfigs.intent: Prompt the student with the live audio tutor to state in their own spoken words what the equal sign tells us about the two sides of a math statement (e.g., 'both sides have the same amount').
componentConfigs.description: Live-judged Direct Instruction practice for ANY skill whose answer is one short SPOKEN word or phrase: the tutor asks a scripted question out loud, the child ANSWERS ALOUD (voice/microphone), and the tutor judges the audio in-band. The stimulus is generated per objective — printed text, a picture, a group of pictures to count, or nothing at all (the tutor says it). Use this when the skill is genuinely verbal and there is NO manipulative the child needs to touch: recall answers, reading a short printed item aloud, counting a group and saying how many, saying which word from a set the objective NAMES (longer/shorter, heavier/lighter) describes two things shown side by side, and — for explain / describe / tell-why objectives — saying IN THEIR OWN WORDS what a shown instance means or what rule it follows (what the equal sign means, the rule of a pattern), judged on meaning rather than wording. ESSENTIAL where a tutor-driven spoken loop is the right modality but no bespoke primitive exists.
evalModeSkills: explain_concept: The child sees one instance (an equation on a balance, a pattern, a ten rod) and says in their own words what it means or what rule it follows. Use for explain / describe / tell-why objectives whose answer is a short idea with many correct wordings. Judged on meaning; the ask never states the concept.

concepts.name: Left Side Blocks
concepts.briefDefinition: A set of identical blocks placed in the left pan to show a starting amount.
concepts.diagramHighlight: The stack of 4 blue blocks resting in the pan on the left side

inContext.scenario: You are building towers with plastic toy blocks at your desk.
inContext.whereToFind: You count out 5 blue blocks and put them in the left scale pan to represent the number 5.

selfCheck.prompt: How would you use physical blocks in the left pan to represent the number 5?
options: Slide 5 loose blocks across the tabletop without touching the scale
Put 1 giant wooden block into the pan to guess the weight
Place a stack of exactly 5 matching blocks into the left pan
selfCheck.hint: Think about counting out the exact number of matching blocks and putting them into that specific pan.

concepts.name: Right Side Blocks
concepts.briefDefinition: The matching blocks you place in the opposite pan to test or create equal weight.
concepts.diagramHighlight: The stack of 4 yellow blocks resting in the pan on the right side

inContext.scenario: You want to share snack crackers equally with a friend using small bowls.
inContext.whereToFind: You count the same number of matching crackers into the right bowl until both bowls match.

selfCheck.prompt: If the left pan holds 3 toy blocks, how can you use blocks on the right side to demonstrate equality?
options: Place exactly 3 matching blocks in the right pan
Leave the right pan empty so it stays high up in the air
Add 8 different heavy items into the right pan
selfCheck.hint: To make both sides equal, you need the exact same count of identical blocks on each side.

concepts.name: Level Balance Beam
concepts.briefDefinition: The straight horizontal bar that stays completely flat when both sides have equal weight.
concepts.diagramHighlight: The straight horizontal bar across the top holding both pans at the same height

inContext.scenario: Two friends who weigh the exact same amount sit on opposite ends of a playground seesaw.
inContext.whereToFind: The seesaw board stays flat across the middle instead of tilting down to the ground on one side.

selfCheck.prompt: What happens to the balance beam when you place 4 blocks on the left and 4 matching blocks on the right?
options: The beam tilts down steeply toward the left floor
The beam rests completely flat and level in a straight horizontal line
The beam flips completely upside down and dumps the blocks
selfCheck.hint: Think about how a level seesaw looks when both ends hold the exact same weight.

cards.title: The Equal Sign (=)
cards.subheading: A Symbol That Means 'The Same Value As'
cards.definition: The equal sign (=) is a math symbol made of two parallel horizontal bars that shows the value on the left side is exactly the same as the value on the right side.

conceptElements.detail: It does not mean 'now do the work' or 'here comes the answer'; it means 'both sides are balanced twins'.
conceptElements.label: True Meaning

conceptElements.detail: Read '=' aloud as 'is the same amount as' to verify whether your math sentence makes sense.
conceptElements.label: Speaking Tip

cards.timelineContext: Introduced into printed mathematics in 1557 to replace writing 'is equal to' by hand.
cards.originStory: Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde grew tired of copying the phrase 'is equal to' again and again. He chose two parallel lines of identical length because nothing could be more equal than a pair of matching straight lines.
cards.curiosityNote: Because '=' just means 'the same as', you can write 5 = 5 or 5 = 2 + 3, and both are completely correct!
cards.visualPrompt: A friendly cartoon equal sign standing between two stacks of colorful counting blocks, with happy eyes indicating that both stacks stand at the exact same height.

cards.title: The Balance Scale
cards.definition: A balance scale is a two-pan measuring tool that sits completely level when both sides hold the exact same amount of weight.

conceptElements.detail: When both pans carry identical amounts, the center beam rests flat without tilting.
conceptElements.label: Level Beam

conceptElements.detail: If one side holds more, that pan drops and the other rises, showing the sides are unequal.
conceptElements.label: The Tilt

conceptElements.detail: The center pivot of a level scale acts just like the equal sign in an equation.
conceptElements.label: Scale as Equal Sign

cards.timelineContext: Used by merchants and builders for more than 4,000 years to ensure honest trading.
cards.originStory: Ancient traders needed a clear visual way to show customers that a purchase was fair. When gold or grain rested level on a balance scale, both sides could agree that the amounts matched perfectly.
cards.curiosityNote: Even a tiny marble added to one balanced pan will instantly tip the beam!
cards.visualPrompt: A brightly colored brass pan scale resting on a classroom desk. The left pan holds four yellow stars and the right pan holds four blue stars. The center beam is perfectly horizontal with an equal sign stamped on the fulcrum.

cards.title: Balanced Equations
cards.definition: A balanced equation is a complete math sentence where the total amount on the left side of the equal sign matches the total amount on the right side.

conceptElements.detail: Left pan can hold '3 + 2' blocks while the right holds '5' blocks; they balance because both total five.
conceptElements.label: Matching Totals

conceptElements.detail: Equations can have math operations on both pans, such as 4 + 1 = 2 + 3.
conceptElements.label: Double-Sided Balance

conceptElements.detail: Because the scale balances either way, 5 = 3 + 2 is just as true as 3 + 2 = 5.
conceptElements.label: Reversible Sides

cards.timelineContext: Core algebraic thinking milestone for elementary math students in grades 1 through 5.
cards.originStory: Math teachers noticed students often guessed wrong when seeing problems like 4 + __ = 7 because they looked for an answer spot. Using balance scales helped students discover that the equal sign requires both sides to weigh the same.
cards.curiosityNote: If you add 2 blocks to the left pan, you must add 2 blocks to the right pan to keep the scale balanced!
cards.visualPrompt: A 3D educational balance beam. The left basket holds two green number blocks marked '3' and '4'. The right basket holds one purple number block marked '7'. The scale rests in perfect horizontal equilibrium.

data.title: Understanding the Equal Sign
data.description: Listen to the math statements and tell us out loud what the equal sign means.
data.gradeLevel: elementary students (grades 1-5) - Use age-appropriate vocabulary, concrete examples, structured learning objectives, and interactive elements. Build fundamental understanding.

items.conceptStatement: Both sides have the same amount.
items.ask: Three plus two equals five. What does the equal sign mean in this math statement?
items.howToPlay: I will show you something, and you tell me what it means in your own words.
items.acceptRule: Any words explaining that the left side and right side match or have the same value count as correct.
items.signatureError: Saying the total number five, or naming the plus sign instead, is NOT an explanation of the equal sign.
items.correctionBody: The equal sign shows that both sides are balanced and have the same amount. Three plus two has the same amount as five.

items.conceptStatement: Both sides have the same amount.
items.ask: Four equals one plus three. What does the equal sign tell us about these two sides?
items.howToPlay: I will show you something, and you tell me what it means in your own words.
items.acceptRule: Any phrasing stating that the two sides balance or show the exact same quantity is accepted.
items.signatureError: Stating that four comes first or that plus means add more is NOT an explanation of the equal sign.
items.correctionBody: The equal sign means both sides are the same. Four is equal in value to one plus three.

items.conceptStatement: Both sides have the same amount.
items.ask: Six equals six. What does the equal sign show us about the number six on the left and the number six on the right?
items.howToPlay: I will show you something, and you tell me what it means in your own words.
items.acceptRule: Any explanation showing that the two numbers are identical or balance each other is correct.
items.signatureError: Just repeating the number six or saying it means the next number is coming is NOT correct.
items.correctionBody: The equal sign tells us that both sides match completely and hold the same amount.

items.conceptStatement: Both sides have the same amount.
items.ask: Two plus four equals one plus five. What does the equal sign mean when we look at both of these expressions?
items.howToPlay: I will show you something, and you tell me what it means in your own words.
items.acceptRule: Any words describing that both sides have equal value or make the same total count as right.
items.signatureError: Saying that six comes next or just reading the numbers aloud is NOT an explanation of the equal sign.
items.correctionBody: The equal sign shows that both sides balance out and have the exact same total amount.

data.intro: Let us look at how a balance scale can hold different groups of blocks that still weigh the exact same amount!

item1.name: Side A: Three and Two
item1.description: This side has a group of 3 blue blocks and a group of 2 red blocks sitting together on the pan.
item1.visualPrompt: A balance scale pan holding three blue blocks and two red blocks, looking happy and even.
points: Shows a group of 3 blocks plus a group of 2 blocks
Makes a total count of 5 blocks

item2.name: Side B: Four and One
item2.description: This side has a group of 4 green blocks and a group of 1 yellow block sitting together on the other pan.
item2.visualPrompt: A balance scale pan holding four green blocks and one yellow block, resting at the exact same level.

synthesis.mainInsight: Even though the groups look different and use different numbers, they both add up to the same total amount, making the scale stay perfectly balanced.
keyDifferences: Side A uses groups of 3 and 2 blocks
Side B uses groups of 4 and 1 blocks
Each side uses different colored blocks
keySimilarities: Both sides add up to a total of 5 blocks
Both pans sit at the exact same level on the balance scale
Both sides show that numbers can be broken into parts in different ways
synthesis.commonMisconception: Students often think that because the groups of numbers look different (3 and 2 versus 4 and 1), one side must be heavier than the other.

whenToUse.item1Context: Use Side A when you want to show how 3 and 2 come together to make 5.
whenToUse.item2Context: Use Side B when you want to show how 4 and 1 come together to make the same 5.

gates.question: Side A uses groups of 3 and 2 blocks, while Side B uses groups of 4 and 1 blocks.
gates.rationale: That is correct! Side A puts together 3 and 2, while Side B puts together 4 and 1, showing two different ways to make groups.

gates.question: Even though the numbers on each side are split differently, both sides make a total of 5 blocks.
gates.rationale: Spot on! Both sides equal 5 in total, which is why the balance scale stays level and even.

data.title: The Great Hanger Balance: Unlocking the Equal Sign
data.subject: Math
data.topic: Understanding the Equal Sign through Concrete Balance
data.overview: Transform an everyday coat hanger and plastic cups into a functioning balance scale to discover what the equal sign really means! Instead of thinking '=' just means 'write the answer', you will physically see how both sides must hold the exact same value to stay level. Test different combinations of coins and tokens to write your own balanced mathematical equations.
learningObjectives: Explain that the equal sign represents a state of balance where both sides hold equal value.
Model balanced equations using different combinations of physical items on a balance scale.
Distinguish between true (balanced) and false (unbalanced) addition equations.

materials.item: Plastic clothes hanger with shoulder notches
substitutes: Wooden hanger with small eyelet screws
A sharpened pencil with adult guidance
Strong tape to attach string to cup sides

steps.title: Prepare the Scale Buckets
steps.instruction: Punch two holes opposite each other near the rim of each plastic cup. Thread a 12-inch piece of yarn through both holes of a cup and tie the ends together to create a sturdy handle loop. Repeat this process for the second cup so both hanging cups are identical.
steps.tip: Make sure the string lengths on both cups are as close to identical as possible so they hang evenly.

steps.title: Assemble and Calibrate the Hanger
steps.instruction: Hang your clothes hanger on a doorknob or handle where it can swing freely. Loop one cup string into the notch on the left arm of the hanger, and the second cup string into the notch on the right arm.

checkpoint.question: Is the hanger bar resting straight and horizontal across before adding any items?

steps.tip: If one side tilts slightly with empty cups, slide the string a fraction of an inch inward or outward until the central bar is straight.

steps.title: Draw the Equal Sign Badge
steps.instruction: Using your marker and an index card, draw a thick, bold equal sign (=). Tape this card right at the center neck of your hanger directly beneath the hook. This reminds us that the center pivot of our balance is where the '=' lives.
steps.scienceNote: In mathematics, the equal sign acts like a balanced seesaw. It does not mean 'do something'; it announces that the quantity on the left side has the exact same value as the quantity on the right side.

steps.title: Test Identical Amounts
steps.instruction: Drop 4 pennies into the left cup. Watch the hanger tip down! Now, add pennies one at a time to the right cup until the hanger levels out straight across again.

checkpoint.question: How many pennies did you have to put in the right cup to bring the hanger back to horizontal?

steps.scienceNote: Because identical pennies have the exact same weight, 4 = 4. The equal sign is satisfied because both sides balance.

steps.title: Model an Addition Expression
steps.instruction: Keep your 4 pennies in the left cup. On your table, split 4 pennies into two groups: 3 pennies and 1 penny. Place the group of 3 pennies and the group of 1 penny together into the right cup.

checkpoint.question: What happened to the hanger balance when you had 4 pennies on one side and 3 + 1 pennies on the other?

steps.scienceNote: Even though the pennies were grouped differently, the total value on each side is identical. You just proved physically that 4 = 3 + 1!

steps.title: Explore Different Combinations
steps.instruction: Place 6 pennies in the left cup. Now test how many different two-part combinations you can put in the right cup to make the hanger balance perfectly. Try 5 + 1, 4 + 2, and 3 + 3.
steps.tip: Wait a few seconds for the hanger to stop swaying before checking if the bar is level.

steps.title: Write Balanced Math Sentences
steps.instruction: Choose your favorite balanced combination from Step 6. On an index card, write the math equation showing what is in the left cup, write '=' in the middle, and write what is in the right cup (for example: '6 = 2 + 4' or '3 + 3 = 4 + 2'). Place the card in front of your scale.

reflectionPrompts.question: When one cup drops lower than the other, what does that tell you about the values on each side, and can we put an '=' between them?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Explain that the equal sign represents a state of balance where both sides hold equal value.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Think about whether a tilted scale means both sides are the same or different.

reflectionPrompts.question: Many math worksheets put an equation like 5 + 2 = ___ with a blank at the end. How does our hanger scale show that an equation can also be written like 7 = 5 + 2 or 4 + 3 = 5 + 2?

concepts.name: Left Side Blocks
concepts.briefDefinition: A set of identical blocks placed in the left pan to show a starting amount.
concepts.diagramHighlight: The stack of 4 blue blocks resting in the pan on the left side

inContext.scenario: You are building towers with plastic toy blocks at your desk.
inContext.whereToFind: You count out 5 blue blocks and put them in the left scale pan to represent the number 5.

selfCheck.prompt: How would you use physical blocks in the left pan to represent the number 5?
options: Slide 5 loose blocks across the tabletop without touching the scale
Put 1 giant wooden block into the pan to guess the weight
Place a stack of exactly 5 matching blocks into the left pan
selfCheck.hint: Think about counting out the exact number of matching blocks and putting them into that specific pan.

concepts.name: Right Side Blocks
concepts.briefDefinition: The matching blocks you place in the opposite pan to test or create equal weight.
concepts.diagramHighlight: The stack of 4 yellow blocks resting in the pan on the right side

inContext.scenario: You want to share snack crackers equally with a friend using small bowls.
inContext.whereToFind: You count the same number of matching crackers into the right bowl until both bowls match.

selfCheck.prompt: If the left pan holds 3 toy blocks, how can you use blocks on the right side to demonstrate equality?
options: Place exactly 3 matching blocks in the right pan
Leave the right pan empty so it stays high up in the air
Add 8 different heavy items into the right pan
selfCheck.hint: To make both sides equal, you need the exact same count of identical blocks on each side.

concepts.name: Level Balance Beam
concepts.briefDefinition: The straight horizontal bar that stays completely flat when both sides have equal weight.
concepts.diagramHighlight: The straight horizontal bar across the top holding both pans at the same height

inContext.scenario: Two friends who weigh the exact same amount sit on opposite ends of a playground seesaw.
inContext.whereToFind: The seesaw board stays flat across the middle instead of tilting down to the ground on one side.

selfCheck.prompt: What happens to the balance beam when you place 4 blocks on the left and 4 matching blocks on the right?
options: The beam tilts down steeply toward the left floor
The beam rests completely flat and level in a straight horizontal line
The beam flips completely upside down and dumps the blocks
selfCheck.hint: Think about how a level seesaw looks when both ends hold the exact same weight.

cards.title: The Equal Sign (=)
cards.subheading: A Symbol That Means 'The Same Value As'
cards.definition: The equal sign (=) is a math symbol made of two parallel horizontal bars that shows the value on the left side is exactly the same as the value on the right side.

conceptElements.detail: It does not mean 'now do the work' or 'here comes the answer'; it means 'both sides are balanced twins'.
conceptElements.label: True Meaning

conceptElements.detail: Read '=' aloud as 'is the same amount as' to verify whether your math sentence makes sense.
conceptElements.label: Speaking Tip

cards.timelineContext: Introduced into printed mathematics in 1557 to replace writing 'is equal to' by hand.
cards.originStory: Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde grew tired of copying the phrase 'is equal to' again and again. He chose two parallel lines of identical length because nothing could be more equal than a pair of matching straight lines.
cards.curiosityNote: Because '=' just means 'the same as', you can write 5 = 5 or 5 = 2 + 3, and both are completely correct!
cards.visualPrompt: A friendly cartoon equal sign standing between two stacks of colorful counting blocks, with happy eyes indicating that both stacks stand at the exact same height.

cards.title: The Balance Scale
cards.definition: A balance scale is a two-pan measuring tool that sits completely level when both sides hold the exact same amount of weight.

conceptElements.detail: When both pans carry identical amounts, the center beam rests flat without tilting.
conceptElements.label: Level Beam

conceptElements.detail: If one side holds more, that pan drops and the other rises, showing the sides are unequal.
conceptElements.label: The Tilt

conceptElements.detail: The center pivot of a level scale acts just like the equal sign in an equation.
conceptElements.label: Scale as Equal Sign

cards.timelineContext: Used by merchants and builders for more than 4,000 years to ensure honest trading.
cards.originStory: Ancient traders needed a clear visual way to show customers that a purchase was fair. When gold or grain rested level on a balance scale, both sides could agree that the amounts matched perfectly.
cards.curiosityNote: Even a tiny marble added to one balanced pan will instantly tip the beam!
cards.visualPrompt: A brightly colored brass pan scale resting on a classroom desk. The left pan holds four yellow stars and the right pan holds four blue stars. The center beam is perfectly horizontal with an equal sign stamped on the fulcrum.

cards.title: Balanced Equations
cards.definition: A balanced equation is a complete math sentence where the total amount on the left side of the equal sign matches the total amount on the right side.

conceptElements.detail: Left pan can hold '3 + 2' blocks while the right holds '5' blocks; they balance because both total five.
conceptElements.label: Matching Totals

conceptElements.detail: Equations can have math operations on both pans, such as 4 + 1 = 2 + 3.
conceptElements.label: Double-Sided Balance

conceptElements.detail: Because the scale balances either way, 5 = 3 + 2 is just as true as 3 + 2 = 5.
conceptElements.label: Reversible Sides

cards.timelineContext: Core algebraic thinking milestone for elementary math students in grades 1 through 5.
cards.originStory: Math teachers noticed students often guessed wrong when seeing problems like 4 + __ = 7 because they looked for an answer spot. Using balance scales helped students discover that the equal sign requires both sides to weigh the same.
cards.curiosityNote: If you add 2 blocks to the left pan, you must add 2 blocks to the right pan to keep the scale balanced!
cards.visualPrompt: A 3D educational balance beam. The left basket holds two green number blocks marked '3' and '4'. The right basket holds one purple number block marked '7'. The scale rests in perfect horizontal equilibrium.

data.title: Understanding the Equal Sign
data.description: Listen to the math statements and tell us out loud what the equal sign means.
data.gradeLevel: elementary students (grades 1-5) - Use age-appropriate vocabulary, concrete examples, structured learning objectives, and interactive elements. Build fundamental understanding.

items.conceptStatement: Both sides have the same amount.
items.ask: Three plus two equals five. What does the equal sign mean in this math statement?
items.howToPlay: I will show you something, and you tell me what it means in your own words.
items.acceptRule: Any words explaining that the left side and right side match or have the same value count as correct.
items.signatureError: Saying the total number five, or naming the plus sign instead, is NOT an explanation of the equal sign.
items.correctionBody: The equal sign shows that both sides are balanced and have the same amount. Three plus two has the same amount as five.

items.conceptStatement: Both sides have the same amount.
items.ask: Four equals one plus three. What does the equal sign tell us about these two sides?
items.howToPlay: I will show you something, and you tell me what it means in your own words.
items.acceptRule: Any phrasing stating that the two sides balance or show the exact same quantity is accepted.
items.signatureError: Stating that four comes first or that plus means add more is NOT an explanation of the equal sign.
items.correctionBody: The equal sign means both sides are the same. Four is equal in value to one plus three.

items.conceptStatement: Both sides have the same amount.
items.ask: Six equals six. What does the equal sign show us about the number six on the left and the number six on the right?
items.howToPlay: I will show you something, and you tell me what it means in your own words.
items.acceptRule: Any explanation showing that the two numbers are identical or balance each other is correct.
items.signatureError: Just repeating the number six or saying it means the next number is coming is NOT correct.
items.correctionBody: The equal sign tells us that both sides match completely and hold the same amount.

items.conceptStatement: Both sides have the same amount.
items.ask: Two plus four equals one plus five. What does the equal sign mean when we look at both of these expressions?
items.howToPlay: I will show you something, and you tell me what it means in your own words.
items.acceptRule: Any words describing that both sides have equal value or make the same total count as right.
items.signatureError: Saying that six comes next or just reading the numbers aloud is NOT an explanation of the equal sign.
items.correctionBody: The equal sign shows that both sides balance out and have the exact same total amount.

data.title: The Balance Scale Friends
data.intro: Let us look at how a balance scale can hold different groups of blocks that still weigh the exact same amount!

item1.name: Side A: Three and Two
item1.description: This side has a group of 3 blue blocks and a group of 2 red blocks sitting together on the pan.
item1.visualPrompt: A balance scale pan holding three blue blocks and two red blocks, looking happy and even.
points: Shows a group of 3 blocks plus a group of 2 blocks
Makes a total count of 5 blocks
Uses two different colors to show the split

item2.name: Side B: Four and One
item2.description: This side has a group of 4 green blocks and a group of 1 yellow block sitting together on the other pan.
item2.visualPrompt: A balance scale pan holding four green blocks and one yellow block, resting at the exact same level.
points: Shows a group of 4 blocks plus a group of 1 block
Makes a total count of 5 blocks
Uses two different colors to show the split

synthesis.mainInsight: Even though the groups look different and use different numbers, they both add up to the same total amount, making the scale stay perfectly balanced.
keyDifferences: Side A uses groups of 3 and 2 blocks
Side B uses groups of 4 and 1 blocks
Each side uses different colored blocks
keySimilarities: Both sides add up to a total of 5 blocks
Both pans sit at the exact same level on the balance scale
Both sides show that numbers can be broken into parts in different ways
synthesis.commonMisconception: Students often think that because the groups of numbers look different (3 and 2 versus 4 and 1), one side must be heavier than the other.

whenToUse.item1Context: Use Side A when you want to show how 3 and 2 come together to make 5.
whenToUse.item2Context: Use Side B when you want to show how 4 and 1 come together to make the same 5.

gates.question: Side A uses groups of 3 and 2 blocks, while Side B uses groups of 4 and 1 blocks.
gates.rationale: That is correct! Side A puts together 3 and 2, while Side B puts together 4 and 1, showing two different ways to make groups.

gates.question: Even though the numbers on each side are split differently, both sides make a total of 5 blocks.
gates.rationale: Spot on! Both sides equal 5 in total, which is why the balance scale stays level and even.

data.title: The Great Hanger Balance: Unlocking the Equal Sign
data.subject: Math
data.topic: Understanding the Equal Sign through Concrete Balance
data.overview: Transform an everyday coat hanger and plastic cups into a functioning balance scale to discover what the equal sign really means! Instead of thinking '=' just means 'write the answer', you will physically see how both sides must hold the exact same value to stay level. Test different combinations of coins and tokens to write your own balanced mathematical equations.
learningObjectives: Explain that the equal sign represents a state of balance where both sides hold equal value.
Model balanced equations using different combinations of physical items on a balance scale.
Distinguish between true (balanced) and false (unbalanced) addition equations.

materials.item: Plastic clothes hanger with shoulder notches
substitutes: Wooden hanger with small eyelet screws
A sharpened pencil with adult guidance
Strong tape to attach string to cup sides

steps.title: Prepare the Scale Buckets
steps.instruction: Punch two holes opposite each other near the rim of each plastic cup. Thread a 12-inch piece of yarn through both holes of a cup and tie the ends together to create a sturdy handle loop. Repeat this process for the second cup so both hanging cups are identical.
steps.tip: Make sure the string lengths on both cups are as close to identical as possible so they hang evenly.

steps.title: Assemble and Calibrate the Hanger
steps.instruction: Hang your clothes hanger on a doorknob or handle where it can swing freely. Loop one cup string into the notch on the left arm of the hanger, and the second cup string into the notch on the right arm.

checkpoint.question: Is the hanger bar resting straight and horizontal across before adding any items?

steps.tip: If one side tilts slightly with empty cups, slide the string a fraction of an inch inward or outward until the central bar is straight.

steps.title: Draw the Equal Sign Badge
steps.instruction: Using your marker and an index card, draw a thick, bold equal sign (=). Tape this card right at the center neck of your hanger directly beneath the hook. This reminds us that the center pivot of our balance is where the '=' lives.
steps.scienceNote: In mathematics, the equal sign acts like a balanced seesaw. It does not mean 'do something'; it announces that the quantity on the left side has the exact same value as the quantity on the right side.

steps.title: Test Identical Amounts
steps.instruction: Drop 4 pennies into the left cup. Watch the hanger tip down! Now, add pennies one at a time to the right cup until the hanger levels out straight across again.

checkpoint.question: How many pennies did you have to put in the right cup to bring the hanger back to horizontal?

steps.scienceNote: Because identical pennies have the exact same weight, 4 = 4. The equal sign is satisfied because both sides balance.

steps.title: Model an Addition Expression
steps.instruction: Keep your 4 pennies in the left cup. On your table, split 4 pennies into two groups: 3 pennies and 1 penny. Place the group of 3 pennies and the group of 1 penny together into the right cup.

checkpoint.question: What happened to the hanger balance when you had 4 pennies on one side and 3 + 1 pennies on the other?

steps.scienceNote: Even though the pennies were grouped differently, the total value on each side is identical. You just proved physically that 4 = 3 + 1!

steps.title: Explore Different Combinations
steps.instruction: Place 6 pennies in the left cup. Now test how many different two-part combinations you can put in the right cup to make the hanger balance perfectly. Try 5 + 1, 4 + 2, and 3 + 3.
steps.tip: Wait a few seconds for the hanger to stop swaying before checking if the bar is level.

steps.title: Write Balanced Math Sentences
steps.instruction: Choose your favorite balanced combination from Step 6. On an index card, write the math equation showing what is in the left cup, write '=' in the middle, and write what is in the right cup (for example: '6 = 2 + 4' or '3 + 3 = 4 + 2'). Place the card in front of your scale.

reflectionPrompts.question: When one cup drops lower than the other, what does that tell you about the values on each side, and can we put an '=' between them?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Explain that the equal sign represents a state of balance where both sides hold equal value.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Think about whether a tilted scale means both sides are the same or different.

reflectionPrompts.question: Many math worksheets put an equation like 5 + 2 = ___ with a blank at the end. How does our hanger scale show that an equation can also be written like 7 = 5 + 2 or 4 + 3 = 5 + 2?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Distinguish between true (balanced) and false (unbalanced) addition equations.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Think about what happened when both cups had combinations that made the scale stay flat.

reflectionPrompts.question: If you put 1 heavy metal button in the left cup and 3 pennies in the right cup, the hanger balances level. Why can 1 object equal 3 objects on our scale?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Model balanced equations using different combinations of physical items on a balance scale.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Consider whether 'equal' always means counting the number of items or measuring their total value or weight.

documentationPrompt.instruction: Take a photo of your hanger scale resting completely level with an interesting combination of items in each cup, placing your handwritten equation card directly beneath it.
documentationPrompt.suggestedCaption: My hanger scale proved that ___ + ___ = ___ because both sides balanced completely level!

extensions.title: The Mystery Object Value Quest
extensions.description: Place one mystery household object (such as a small eraser, key, or crayon) into the left cup. Add pennies to the right cup one by one until the scale balances perfectly. Write an equation showing the item's 'penny value' (e.g., 1 Eraser = 7 Pennies).

extensions.title: True or False Detective
extensions.description: Have a family member write three equations on cards (e.g., 3 + 2 = 6, 4 + 1 = 2 + 3, and 5 + 0 = 4 + 2). Test each equation by loading the hanger cups with the exact quantities shown on both sides. Label each card as 'TRUE (Balanced)' or 'FALSE (Tilted)'.

safetyNotes: Adult supervision recommended when using scissors or a hole punch to pierce plastic cups.
Choking hazard: Small coins, buttons, and beans should be handled with care and kept away from young children under 3 years old.
Ensure the hanger is secured on a stable hook or handle so it does not slip off during testing.

problems.question: Which scale shows that both sides are equal?
problems.rationale: Scale A has 3 apples on each side, so both sides are equal. An equal sign means both sides have the same value.
problems.teachingNote: Remind students that equal means having the same amount on both sides. A scale stays level when both pans are balanced.
successCriteria: Identify when two sides of a balance scale are equal
Recognize that equal means the same amount on both sides

problems.question: Why does the scale stay balanced?
problems.rationale: Both sides have four blocks in all. Equal means having the same total amount even if the colors look different.
problems.teachingNote: Young learners often believe groups must look identical to be equal. Reinforce that the equal sign means having the same quantity, not the same appearance.
successCriteria: Explain that balance scales are level when both sides have the same total
Recognize that equal amounts can look different
